newsitem.title: USA: US July retail sales show consumers back from lull.
newsitem.headline: US July retail sales show consumers back from lull.

text.p: U.S. consumer spending kicked off the second-half of the year on a good, although not spectacular, note, leading analysts to believe that the slowdown in consumption seen earlier in the year is over.
The Commerce Department on Wednesday reported that retail sales rose 0.6 percent in July against a revised 0.7 percent rise in June. Sales excluding autos were up 0.5 percent.
The data were mostly in line with Wall Street expectations, which had called for a 0.7 percent increase in overall sales and a 0.5 percent rise in sales ex-autos.
"The numbers are solid, but not out of the ordinary," said Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi. "We are now getting a return to trend after a soft second quarter."
A 0.6 percent increase, he added, is about where retail sales should be at the current stage of the business cycle, in which the economic expansion is in its seventh year.

Although the data came as expected, many analysts had feared an incraese of 1.0 percent or above. The U.S. Treasury market was relieved when the gloomiest forecasts did not materialize, analysts said.
Bonds also rallied after the producer price index for July, which was also released on Wednesday, fell for the seventh straight month.
Bond prices surged about 1-1/4 points after the double-dose of data pointed to a benign inflation environment and a solid, but nowhere near overheating, economy.

Retail sales ended the second quarter on a stronger note than previously thought, as June numbers were revised upward to show an overall retail sales gain of 0.7 percent gain from up 0.5 percent previously and an ex-autos rise of 0.4 percent from up 0.3 percent earlier.
Following two "reasonably good" months, "the focus will shift to August to see what will happen to August retail sales," said Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp.

Niemira said that with consumer fundamentals remaining solid -- including strong job and income growth -- spending should pickup further throughout the third quarter and rebound sharply in the fourth quarter.
The July retail sales data showed very little surprises, although auto sales -- up 1.0 percent -- were not as strong as many economists predicted based on very healthy July unit sales.
Some said that the retail sales report did not fully reflect the solid auto sales picture in July, and thus will show a upward revision next month.

Yet others argued that the auto unit numbers have not tracked well with retail sales in recent months. Units may be higher, but due to heavy incentives and discounting the price of an automobile is lower, they explained.

One caveat is the 10-day old United Parcel Service (UPS) strike, which could hamper some sales should it continue much longer. But analysts said that it is still too soon to determine the strike's effect on sales.

All other components in the July report posted gains except furniture store sales, which fell 0.4 percent. Analysts said that furniture store sales are soft, as are computer sales, which make up half of the category.
"When you look at the (overall retail sales number), it's rising at a moderate rate, which confirms the consumer is back," said Astrid Adolfson, senior vice president at MCM MoneyWatch.
"(But they are) not spending at a five or six percent rate, but more likely at a two to three percent (rate) that the Federal Reserve is comfortable with."
